items.prompt: Which writing system is mainly used for foreign loanwords such as コーヒー (coffee)?

options.label: Kanji
Romaji
Hiragana
Katakana

rubric: Katakana is the script used mainly for loanwords.
Hiragana is for native grammar words and endings, so it is the common mix-up.

items.prompt: How is the kanji 水 (water) read in the word みず?

options.label: みず
き
つち
ひ

rubric: 水 means water and is read みず.
ひ (fire), き (tree) and つち (earth) are other basic element kanji that learners confuse with it.

items.prompt: Which particle marks the topic of a sentence, as in わたしは がくせいです?

options.label: で
は
を
に

rubric: は marks the topic.
を marks the direct object, so it is the most common confusion.

items.prompt: What does ありがとう mean?

options.label: Good morning
Thank you
I'm sorry
Goodbye

rubric: ありがとう means thank you.
Other options are different common phrases (すみません, おはよう, さようなら).

items.prompt: What does the kanji 川 mean?

options.label: Mountain
Rice field
River
Sun

rubric: 川 means river.
山 (mountain), 田 (rice field) and 日 (sun) are similar beginner kanji that are often mixed up with it.

items.prompt: Which of these characters are hiragana? Select all that apply.

options.label: シ
あ
し
ア
日

rubric: あ and し are hiragana.
ア and シ are katakana lookalike sounds; 日 is kanji.

items.prompt: A traveller in Japan wants to take a train. At the street corner she sees a large sign with the single kanji 駅 and a train symbol. Her phrasebook lists the word as basic vocabulary. What does 駅 mean?

options.label: Hospital
Exit
Park
Station

rubric: 駅 means station.
Hospital (病院), park (公園) and exit (出口) are other common sign words learners confuse.

items.prompt: In わたしは がくせいです, why is the character は pronounced "wa" and not "ha"?

options.label: It is a katakana character that always has the sound wa in any word
It is the topic particle, written は but pronounced wa
It is a regional accent that changes ha to wa in every word of the sentence
It follows わたし, so the sound shifts to match the preceding vowel

rubric: Topic particle は is pronounced wa by rule.
Distractors treat it as a general sound change rather than a particle rule.

items.prompt: Which is the polite negative form of いきます (to go)?

options.label: いきました
いきない
いきません
いきませた

rubric: Polite negative replaces ます with ません.
いきない mixes plain endings with polite stem; いきました is past.

items.prompt: What does か at the end of がくせいですか do?

options.label: It makes the sentence past tense
It makes the sentence negative
It marks the sentence as a command
It turns the sentence into a question

rubric: Sentence-final か forms a question.
Other options attribute tense, negation or command meaning to it.

items.prompt: Which of these words is an い-adjective?

options.label: げんき (healthy)
たかい (tall)
しずか (quiet)
きれい (pretty)

rubric: たかい ends in い and conjugates as an い-adjective.
きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective, the common trap.

items.prompt: What is the difference in meaning between おばさん and おばあさん?

options.label: Grandmother versus aunt
Mother versus aunt
Aunt versus grandmother
Sister versus mother

rubric: The long vowel changes the word: おばさん is aunt, おばあさん is grandmother.
The reversed option swaps the meanings; others show the length is ignored.

items.prompt: Which sentences are in the polite (です/ます) style? Select all that apply.

options.label: パンを たべる。
わたしは いく。
これは ほんです。
あした がっこうへ いきます。

rubric: です and ます endings mark polite style.
いく and たべる are plain dictionary forms.

items.prompt: A learner writes a message to a friend: きのう とうきょうを いきました (meaning "I went to Tokyo yesterday"). Her teacher says one particle is wrong. Which particle should replace を to mark the destination?

options.label: が
で
に
の

rubric: に (or へ) marks the destination of movement verbs.
で marks the place of an action, the usual confusion.

items.prompt: In the sentence 私は学生です, what is the role of the particle は?

options.label: It marks the destination of movement
It marks the place where an action happens
It marks the direct object of the verb
It marks the topic the sentence is about

rubric: は marks the topic, here 'as for me'.
Distractors confuse は with を (object), へ/に (destination) and で (location of action).

items.prompt: Which of these words is a な-adjective, even though it ends in い?

options.label: たかい
おいしい
あたらしい
きれい

rubric: きれい (pretty, clean) takes な: きれいな人.
The other three are true い-adjectives; learners assume every word ending in い is one.

items.prompt: Which word would normally be written in katakana?

options.label: 本
やま
コーヒー
水

rubric: Katakana is used for loanwords such as コーヒー (coffee).
The others are native or Chinese-origin words written in kanji or hiragana.

items.prompt: What does 昨日はケーキを食べませんでした mean?

options.label: I do not eat cake usually
I was not eating cake then
I will not eat cake tomorrow
I did not eat cake yesterday

rubric: 〜ませんでした is the polite past negative, and 昨日 means yesterday.
Distractors misread the tense: future, habitual and progressive.

items.prompt: Why is the particle で used in 学校で友達に会いました?

options.label: It marks the person who was met
It marks the place of the action
It marks the time the meeting took place
It marks the direction of movement toward a goal

rubric: で marks the location of an action; 友達に marks the person met.
Distractors mix up で with に (person, time) and へ (direction).

items.prompt: Which of these verb forms are in the polite (ます) style? Select all that apply.

options.label: 行きました
見ない
食べます
飲む

rubric: 食べます and 行きました are polite forms, present and past.
飲む and 見ない are plain forms (dictionary and plain negative).

items.prompt: Your host family leaves you a note: 「今日は友達と映画を見に行きます。晩ごはんは冷蔵庫にあります。」 What does the note tell you?

options.label: They are going to see a movie with a friend today, and dinner is in the fridge
They are going to meet a friend at the theater, and dinner is being cooked
They are going to a movie alone today, and dinner is on the table
They saw a movie with a friend yesterday, and dinner is in the fridge

rubric: 今日 is today, 友達と is with a friend, 行きます is future/present polite, 冷蔵庫に is in the fridge.
Distractors change who goes, the tense or the dinner location.

items.prompt: What is the correct て-form of 飲む (to drink)?

options.label: 飲きて
飲いて
飲って
飲んで

rubric: Verbs ending in む change to んで.
Other forms apply the wrong group rule, such as the う/つ/る or く pattern.

items.prompt: How do you say 'It was not expensive' politely, using 高い (expensive)?

options.label: 高くなかったです
高くないでした
高いじゃなかったです
高かったじゃないです

rubric: い-adjectives form the past negative as 〜くなかったです.
Distractors use the な-adjective pattern or mix the past and negative endings.

items.prompt: Choose the particle that fits: 私は毎朝バス（　）学校に行きます。

options.label: が
を
に
で

rubric: で marks the means of transport.
に is tempting because of the destination, but it doesn't mark means; を and が don't fit.

items.prompt: Which phrase correctly says 'I have two cats'?

options.label: 猫が二本います
猫が二匹います
猫が二枚います
猫が二人います

rubric: Small animals are counted with 匹.
人 is for people, 枚 for flat things and 本 for long objects.

items.prompt: How do you read 三百円 (300 yen)?

options.label: さんぴゃくえん
さんびゃくえん
さんひゃくえん
みっひゃくえん

rubric: After 三, 百 becomes びゃく: さんびゃく.
Distractors use the unvoiced ひゃく, the ぴゃく of 六/八, or a wrong number reading.

items.prompt: Which sentences are grammatically correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: 駅で友達に会いました。
学校を行きます。
図書館に本を読みます。
日本語を勉強します。

rubric: The first uses を for the object; the third uses で for the action location and に for the person met.
学校を行きます should use へ/に, and 図書館に本を読みます should use で for the location.

items.prompt: Your host mother asks about your weekend. You want to say you went to Kyoto by train with a friend last weekend. Which sentence do you use?

options.label: 先週末、友達と電車で京都へ行きました。
先週末、友達を電車に京都で行きます。
先週末、友達と電車で京都を行きます。
先週末、友達で電車と京都へ行きました。

rubric: と marks the companion, で the means, へ the destination, and ました the past.
Distractors misuse particles or leave the verb in the non-past.

items.prompt: Which is the correct te-form of the verb 行く (iku, 'to go')?

options.label: 行って
行んで
行いて
行きて

rubric: 行く is the one irregular case among the -く verbs: its te-form is 行って, not 行いて.
行いて applies the regular 書く→書いて pattern, which is the common overgeneralisation.

items.prompt: Choose the particle that completes the sentence: 駅___ 友達に会いました。 ('I met a friend at the station.')

options.label: で
を
へ
に

rubric: で marks the place where an action happens, and meeting is an action done at the station.
に is the common wrong pick because it also marks locations, but it marks where something exists or a destination.

items.prompt: Which is the correct plain past negative of the i-adjective 高い (takai, 'expensive')?

options.label: 高くなかった
高くないでした
高かったない
高いじゃなかった

rubric: An i-adjective drops い, adds くなかった for the plain past negative.
高いじゃなかった applies the noun/na-adjective pattern to an i-adjective.

items.prompt: How do you read 三本 when counting three pencils?

options.label: さんもと
さんほん
さんぽん
さんぼん

rubric: After 三, the counter 本 is voiced to ぼん.
さんぽん is the pattern for 一, 六, 八 and 十, so it is the commonly confused pick.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I want to eat sushi' in polite Japanese?

options.label: 寿司が食べるたいです
寿司が食べたいます
寿司が食べたいです
寿司が食べたくないです

rubric: The stem 食べ plus たい makes an i-adjective, so the polite ending is です.
食べたいます wrongly attaches ます to the adjective, and 食べるたい keeps the dictionary form instead of the stem.

items.prompt: Which of these sentences correctly use the polite past tense? Select all that apply.

options.label: 先週は忙しかったです
昨日は雨でした
朝ご飯を食べるました
昨日映画を見ました
昨日は暇くなかったです

rubric: Verbs use stem+ました, i-adjectives use かったです, and nouns use でした.
暇 is a na-adjective, so 暇くなかったです mixes patterns, and 食べるました keeps the dictionary ending.

items.prompt: You are staying with a host family in Japan and send them a short polite message. You want to say that after dinner you will go to the supermarket. Which sentence should you write?

options.label: 晩ご飯の後で、スーパーを行きます
晩ご飯を後で、スーパーへ行ったです
晩ご飯の後で、スーパーに行きます
晩ご飯の前で、スーパーに行きます

rubric: The destination of 行く takes に (or へ), and 後で marks 'after'.
Using を with 行く and 前 (before) are slips that change the grammar or meaning.

items.prompt: A learner writes 「昨日、友達に会うました」. What is the cause of the error?

options.label: 会う is a u-verb, so ます must attach to the stem 会い rather than to the dictionary form
友達に is the faulty part because meeting someone always requires the particle を
会う is an irregular verb, so it must change to 会しました in the polite past
ました can only follow verbs ending in る, so 会う needs a different final ending

rubric: Polite forms attach to the masu-stem, so 会います/会いました is correct.
The distractors misclassify the verb or blame the particle, though 会う correctly takes に.

items.prompt: In the question 「誰がコーヒーを飲みますか」, why is 誰 marked with が rather than は?

options.label: は cannot follow any question word because question words are always objects of verbs
誰 is the unknown focus of the question, and が marks the new information being asked for
は marks the person doing the action, while が marks the thing that is being drunk
が is the polite particle, so questions to strangers must use が instead of は

rubric: が marks new or focused information, which is exactly what a question word asks for.
The distractors invent politeness rules or reverse the roles of は and が.

items.prompt: Which word has a reading that cannot be built from the usual on'yomi or kun'yomi of its individual kanji?

options.label: 大学
学生
日本語
今日

rubric: 今日 (きょう) is an irregular reading for the whole word, not a combination of the standard readings of 今 and 日.
The other words are built from regular readings of their kanji.

items.prompt: A learner texts their teacher 「先生、明日宿題を出すよ。」 What is the main problem?

options.label: The plain verb plus sentence-final よ is too casual a register for a teacher
出す is the wrong verb because 宿題 can only be used with やる in writing
Tomorrow needs a counter such as 一日 before the verb in polite messages
The particle を should be は because 宿題 is the topic of every sentence

rubric: Politeness is carried by the verb form and sentence-final particles, so 出します would suit a teacher.
The distractors blame verb choice, particles or counters, which are fine here.

items.prompt: What does 「窓が開いています」 most naturally describe?

options.label: The window is being opened by someone right now
The window will be opened by someone in the near future
The window is in an open state after having been opened
The window is regularly opened at a fixed time each day

rubric: An intransitive verb with ている usually describes a resulting state.
Learners who treat ている as only 'in progress' pick the first option.

items.prompt: A learner writes 「昨日は雨が降るでした」. Which statements correctly explain why it is wrong? Select all that apply.

options.label: The polite past of a verb is formed from the stem plus ました, giving 降りました
でした is the polite past of the copula for nouns and na-adjectives, not something attached to a plain verb
降る is irregular, so it has no polite past form and needs a different verb
雨 must be marked with を because it is what is being fallen

rubric: Verbs form the polite past with ました, while でした belongs to nouns and na-adjectives.
降る is a regular u-verb and 雨 correctly takes が, so the other statements are wrong.

items.prompt: At a post office, a learner asks for a stamp but says 「きてをください」. The clerk looks confused. The learner meant 切手 (stamp). What best explains the misunderstanding?

options.label: Dropping the small っ turned きって into きて, which is a different word meaning 'come'
The learner wrote the word in hiragana, which clerks cannot understand in speech
The learner confused the pitch of the word, since pitch alone separates きって from きて
The learner used the wrong particle, because ください should follow に rather than を

rubric: The small っ marks a doubled consonant, which changes the word's length and identity.
The distractors point to particles, pitch or script, none of which explains the change from 切手 to きて.

items.prompt: A learner tells a client on the phone 「部長は今いらっしゃいません」 about their own department head. What is the main error?

options.label: 部長 must become 部長さん, because a title needs さん to sound polite to a client
いません is required here, because keigo is never used toward clients on the phone
いらっしゃる is a humble verb, so the sentence accidentally lowers the client instead of the head
いらっしゃる honors the head, but to outsiders one's own superior is lowered, so おりません fits

rubric: In uchi/soto usage, one's own superior is referred to humbly toward outsiders, so いらっしゃる is wrong.
Distractors confuse honorific with humble verbs or assume titles need さん.

items.prompt: Someone asks 「だれが来ましたか。」 Which reply is natural, and why?

options.label: 田中さんも来ました, because も is the default particle for answering questions
田中さんを来ました, because the answer is the object of the question
田中さんが来ました, because が marks the unknown answer to the question word
田中さんは来ました, because は marks the new information the asker wants to hear

rubric: A question word takes が, and the answer carrying the new information also takes が.
は would treat 田中さん as known topic; を and も change the meaning.

items.prompt: A learner says 「電気が消しています」 to report that the light is off. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: 電気 needs の before が when it is the subject of a continuing state
が should be に, because 電気 is the place where the action happens
ています cannot attach to 消す at all, because it is an instant verb
消す is transitive and clashes with が; 電気が消えています describes the state

rubric: The transitive/intransitive pair 消す/消える matters: a state of the light being off uses 消えている.
Distractors invent particle or aspect rules that do not apply.

items.prompt: A learner writes 「駅に着くと、電話してください」. Why is it faulty?

options.label: 電話する needs を, so the sentence lacks an object marker and breaks
と clauses cannot lead into a request or the speaker's intention, so 着いたら fits better
ください cannot follow a clause with に, because に blocks later requests
と must follow a past-tense verb, so the learner needed 着いたと for correct grammar

rubric: と expresses automatic or natural consequence and cannot precede requests or volition; たら can.
Distractors invent tense or particle constraints.

items.prompt: A learner says 「友達が来ています」 meaning 'my friend is on the way'. Why does the meaning not match?

options.label: ています only expresses habits, so it cannot describe any single moment right now
ています is the future tense for movement verbs, so it says the friend will arrive later
が turns the sentence into the past, so it says the friend already left
来ています is a resulting state: the friend has arrived and is here; 向かっています fits

rubric: With instant-change verbs like 来る, ている shows the resulting state, not progress.
Distractors misassign tense or habit meanings to ている.

items.prompt: Which sentences use the giving and receiving verbs with correct direction? Select all that apply.

options.label: 私は友達に本を貸してあげました
友達が私に本をあげました
母は私にプレゼントをくれました
私は弟にお菓子をくれました

rubric: くれる is for someone giving to the speaker, and あげる for the speaker giving outward.
Options 2 and 4 reverse the directions.

items.prompt: A learner hears her host brother say 「昨日、雨に降られて大変だった」. She assumes the passive is honorific toward the rain. How should the form 降られて be analysed?

options.label: It is a spontaneous passive meaning the rain fell untouched by anyone, with no effect
It is an adversative passive: the speaker was negatively affected by the rain falling
It is an honorific passive, which shows respect to the rain as the subject of the clause
It is a potential form meaning the rain was able to fall, so the day went well

rubric: The 'suffering passive' marks an event that inconvenienced the speaker, even with intransitive verbs.
Distractors take other uses of られる that do not fit 大変だった.

items.prompt: A peer claims 'は marks the subject and が marks the object.' Judged on accuracy across common sentence types, which critique is best?

options.label: Mostly wrong: が marks the topic and は marks new information, so the peer has the two particles' roles reversed
Mostly wrong: は and が differ mainly in formality, with が used in polite speech and は in casual speech, so no rule is needed
Largely right: は marks the subject and を marks the object, so 水が飲みたい is the only pattern where が replaces を
Partly right at best: は marks a topic, and が marks a subject or a desired object, as in 水が飲みたい

rubric: は marks a topic, which may be subject or object, while が marks subjects and objects of desire or ability.
Distractors reverse roles or deny any difference.

items.prompt: An apology email to a customer for a late delivery must be formal, accept responsibility and not sound like an excuse. Which opening is best?

options.label: 在庫が切れていたんだから、仕方ありません。ごめんなさい
在庫が切れていたので、遅れてしまいました。すみません
在庫の確認が遅れたため、お届けが遅くなり申し訳ございません
在庫が切れていたから、遅れました。申し訳ないです

rubric: ため with 申し訳ございません is formal and owns the delay.
Distractors use casual から/ので with weak apologies or blame.

items.prompt: A learner has three months, 30 minutes a day, and wants to read menus and signs while travelling in Japan. Which plan best fits these limits?

options.label: Learn the 2,000 jōyō kanji in frequency order first, since kanji carry most of the meaning on signs and menus
Learn hiragana and katakana, then add kanji only when a sign is met, since most signs also carry romaji
Learn both kana sets, then about 100 common kanji for food and transit, since signs mix them
Learn hiragana and about 500 kanji, since katakana words on menus can be guessed from context and pictures

rubric: Kana plus a small high-frequency kanji set suits the short timeframe and target texts.
Distractors overreach, rely on romaji or wrongly drop katakana.

items.prompt: A new employee ends a self-introduction with 「よろしくお願いします」. Judged by natural tone and the goodwill it conveys, which English rendering is best?

options.label: I request your order from today on
I ask you to do everything for me
I look forward to working with you
Nice to meet you, and goodbye now

rubric: The phrase asks for goodwill and cooperation; 'look forward to working with you' captures that naturally.
Distractors are literal or mismatched in meaning.

items.prompt: A learner says: 'To be safe, always use あなた for the listener.' Judged by politeness norms toward superiors and acquaintances, which evaluation is best?

options.label: Poor advice: あなた can sound distant or rude, so name+さん or a title is safer
Sound advice: あなた is a neutral, respectful pronoun that suits superiors and strangers
Sound advice: using a pronoun avoids presuming a status, while names suggest undue closeness
Mixed advice: あなた suits superiors, but name+さん is better for peers and close friends

rubric: Name+さん or a title is the safer norm; あなた can sound distant or blunt toward superiors.
Distractors treat あなた as universally polite.

items.prompt: A learner writes to a landlord: 「私は水が出ません。私は昨日から困っています。私は直してほしい。」 Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: 水が出ません is wrong because が cannot mark 水; を is needed
困っています is wrong because ています cannot describe a continuing state
直してほしい is too blunt for a landlord; a request like 直していただけませんか fits
Repeating 私は in every sentence is unnatural, and the topic could be dropped

rubric: Register is too plain, and repeated 私は is unnatural, even making the first sentence say 'I produce no water'.
が is correct for 水, and 困っています correctly shows a continuing state.

items.prompt: A junior employee has a fever and must text the manager before work. Criteria: polite, brief, states the reason and asks permission. Which message is best?

options.label: 熱があるから休みます。よろしくお願いします
熱があって休みたいです。よろしく
体調不良のため、本日お休みをいただけますでしょうか。申し訳ありません
風邪っぽいので、休むかもしれません。すみません

rubric: It states the reason, asks permission in humble form and apologises briefly.
Distractors are too casual, vague or announce the absence instead of asking.

items.prompt: A teacher analyses the sentence 「象は鼻が長い」. Which analysis is best supported by Japanese grammar?

options.label: 象 is the topic marked by は, and 鼻 is the subject of 長い, so the sentence describes elephants by a trait
The sentence is ungrammatical, because only one noun in a clause may carry a particle like は or が
象 is the subject and 鼻が marks an object, because 長い takes a direct object like a transitive verb does
は is the subject marker here, and が is a stylistic variant that can replace it with no change in meaning

rubric: は marks the topic (elephants) and が marks the subject of the adjective 長い (the nose), giving a topic-comment description.
Distractors treat 長い as transitive or は and が as interchangeable, ignoring the topic/subject distinction.

items.prompt: In an email to a client you say you will visit their office tomorrow. Judged by keigo criteria (humble form for your own action, respect toward the client), which verb is best?

options.label: お越しになります
いらっしゃいます
参ります
行かれます

rubric: 参ります is kenjōgo, which lowers your own action and so shows respect to the client.
The other options are honorific forms meant for the client's actions, and using them for yourself raises your own status.

items.prompt: A learner was told: 'To be polite to a superior, always say あなた.' Which critique of this advice is best?

options.label: Wrong: あなた to a superior sounds distant or presumptuous, so the natural choice is the person's name plus title, like 田中部長
Right: あなた is the polite second-person pronoun, and using name plus title would sound overly familiar toward a superior
Wrong: superiors should be addressed with きみ, because it is the pronoun that signals respect toward someone senior to you
Partly right: あなた suits superiors in writing, where its nuance is neutralised and it always reads as polite and formal

rubric: Japanese usually avoids あなた for superiors and uses name plus title instead.
Distractors treat あなた as a safe honorific or confuse きみ, which is used toward juniors, with a respectful form.

items.prompt: A learner has six months and wants to read short news articles. Judging by efficiency and long-term retention, which kanji plan is best?

options.label: Read romaji news at first and add kanji later, since vocabulary and grammar can be built in romaji before the script is tackled
Memorise the 2,136 jōyō kanji in stroke-count order with one reading each, since broad coverage of characters supports reading ability
Learn high-frequency kanji inside words and sentences, picking up on and kun readings through compounds as they recur
Write each kanji many times at the start, since solid stroke order and handwriting practice help characters stick in memory

rubric: Learning frequent kanji in vocabulary context builds readings and meaning together, which suits a reading goal.
Distractors favour isolated memorisation, writing drills or romaji, which do not build reading fluency within the time limit.

items.prompt: A beginner wants to read menus and signs in Japan within a month and to pronounce words accurately. Judged by these two criteria, which plan for romaji is best?

options.label: Stay with romaji for the first year, since it maps one-to-one onto kana sounds and so avoids any pronunciation errors
Learn hiragana and katakana first, since romaji hides distinctions like long vowels and moraic ん and is absent on real signs
Learn kanji first, since signs and menus mostly use kanji and the kana can be absorbed later from furigana alone
Learn only katakana first, since menus and signs use it throughout and hiragana matters only for grammar at a later stage

rubric: Kana are needed for real signage and encode length and mora distinctions that romaji blurs.
Distractors overrate romaji, or wrongly claim signs use only katakana or only kanji.

items.prompt: Your boss invites you to dinner on a night you are busy. You want to decline in a way that is polite, softened and not a blunt rejection. Which refusals fit these criteria? Select all that apply.

options.label: その日は少し都合がつかないのですが、また誘っていただけると嬉しいです。
行きたくないので、今回は遠慮しておきます。
無理です。ほかの日にしてください。
あいにくその日は先約がございまして、申し訳ございません。

rubric: Both correct options give a soft reason and an apology or openness to future invitations, in polite register.
The distractors are blunt or give a direct negative reason or an imperative, which breaks the softening criterion.

items.prompt: A graduate student ends an email to a professor with 「ご苦労様です」, meaning to show respect for the professor's work. A senior classmate is asked to evaluate this choice. Which evaluation is most accurate?

options.label: Inappropriate: it is traditionally used toward equals or juniors, so お世話になっております suits a professor better
Inappropriate only because of ご; plain 苦労様です would be correct for a professor in a formal email
Appropriate: ご苦労様 carries the honorific ご, so it is the standard way to thank a superior for their effort
Appropriate in email, since written Japanese ignores the direction of status that matters in spoken greetings

rubric: ご苦労様 is traditionally said by a higher-status person to a lower one, so お世話になっております is the safer opening or closing toward a professor.
Distractors assume the honorific prefix makes it respectful and ignore the direction of status.

items.prompt: You must ask a stranger to take your photo. Which sentence best meets all constraints: a request, not an imperative, politely asking about their willingness, with you receiving the favour?

options.label: 写真をお撮りになりませんか。
写真を撮ってくださいませんでした。
写真を撮らせていただけませんか。
写真を撮っていただけませんか。

rubric: 〜ていただけませんか politely asks someone to do a favour for you.
撮らせて reverses the meaning (let me take), お撮りになりませんか invites them to take their own photo, and the last is past tense.

items.prompt: In a formal report you must state that you met your professor yesterday, lowering your own act (humble form) and using the past tense. Which sentence meets both constraints?

options.label: 昨日、先生に会われました。
昨日、先生にお会いされました。
昨日、先生にお会いになりました。
昨日、先生にお会いしました。

rubric: お会いしました is the humble form of 会う in the past tense, with you as the actor.
The other options use honorific patterns that raise the actor, which is wrong when the actor is you.

items.prompt: You are building a pronunciation drill for a learner who confuses long and short vowels. Which set contains only pairs that differ solely by vowel length?

options.label: おじさん/おじいさん and ビル/ビール
かく/かぐ and さか/さが and ぶた/ぶだ
しき/しんき and かい/かん and ほし/ほんし
きた/きった and さか/さっか and いち/いっち

rubric: おじさん/おじいさん and ビル/ビール differ only by an added long-vowel mora.
The distractors contrast voicing, geminate consonants, or the moraic nasal, which are different phonological features.

items.prompt: You are closing an email to a client, asking them to review an attached file. Choose the line that makes a soft request with the client as the honoured person doing the checking.

options.label: 添付をご確認させていただけますと幸いです。
添付をご確認なさっていただけますと幸いです。
添付を確認してもらえるとうれしいです。
添付をご確認いただけますと幸いです。

rubric: ご確認いただけますと幸いです is a standard soft request in which the client does the checking.
Distractors are too casual, double honorific, or use a humble causative that means you check.

items.prompt: The sentence 「太郎は花子と次郎に会った」 is ambiguous. Which rewrite unambiguously means that Taro, together with Hanako, met Jiro?

options.label: 太郎は花子と次郎とに会った。
太郎は花子や次郎などに会った。
太郎は花子と一緒に次郎に会った。
太郎は次郎と花子の二人に会った。

rubric: Adding 一緒に makes 花子 a companion, while 次郎 alone is the person met.
The others still allow or require reading both people as the ones met.

items.prompt: You must rewrite the blunt 「これを直して」 for a client. Constraints: it must be a request, not a command, and in polite register suitable for a client. Which rewrites meet them? Select all that apply.

options.label: こちらを直してもらえる？
お手数ですが、こちらをお直しいただけますでしょうか。
こちらを直していただけませんか。
こちらを直しなさい。

rubric: Both correct options are polite request forms with an honorific pattern directed at the client.
The distractors are a command and a casual request, which fail the register constraint.

items.prompt: You live in an apartment and made noise late at night. You leave a handwritten note for a neighbour you barely know. It must apologise, promise future care, and use polite but not excessively stiff Japanese. Which note best meets these constraints?

options.label: 夜遅くに騒がせていただき、ありがとうございました。今後も気をつけます。
夜遅くに騒いでしまい、申し訳ありません。今後は気をつけます。
夜遅くに騒いでごめんね。次からは静かにするから、許してね。
騒いだことを謝罪申し上げる所存でございます。今後は十分に注意いたします。

rubric: The key apologises, gives a commitment, and keeps a polite register that suits a neighbour.
Distractors are too casual, too stiff and incomplete, or wrongly thank the neighbour instead of apologising.
